title: Developmental Psychology Adventure 2: Attachment (Bowlby & Ainsworth)
welcome_lead: Today you'll meet Bowlby's attachment theory and Ainsworth's Strange Situation.
meta_desc: Psychology Developmental: Bowlby's attachment theory and Ainsworth's Strange Situation classifications.
final_note: You explained Bowlby's monotropy and Ainsworth's three attachment classifications.

walkthroughs.body_html:
John Bowlby (1969) argued attachment is an evolved survival mechanism.

A child forms one primary bond (monotropy) within a critical period (~6 mo to 2 yr).

The bond shapes an internal working model guiding all later relationships.

44 Thieves (Bowlby 1944) — 'maternal deprivation' linked to later affectionless psychopathy.

12-month-olds observed across 8 episodes: separations and reunions with caregiver and a stranger.

Three classifications:
- Type B (Secure): 60–70% in US.
- Type A (Insecure-avoidant): ignores caregiver.
- Type C (Insecure-resistant): clingy and angry.

Later Type D (disorganised) added by Main & Solomon (1986).

van IJzendoorn & Kroonenberg (1988) meta-analysis of 8 countries: B universally most common but rates varied — more Type A in Germany, more Type C in Japan and Israel.

Critique: Strange Situation is an imposed etic; conclusions about 'insecure' may reflect cultural child-rearing norms.
